strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.26	written Torah as witness	The commentary treats Abraham's and Moses' first pages as a durable warning; Deuteronomy puts Moses' written Torah beside the ark as a witness against Israel, making the old text itself testimony.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.19	written song taught by heart	Moses is told to write a song and put it in Israel's mouths as a witness; this joins the commentary's two preservations, written pages and words retained by recitation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.30.8	warning written for the future	Isaiah is commanded to inscribe a warning in a book for future days as a lasting witness, closely matching the commentary's old pages whose warning remains present.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.8	grass fades, divine word endures	The commentary places the dried pasture beside pages that have not vanished; Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flower with God's word standing forever.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.23	royal destruction of a scroll	Jehoiakim cuts and burns Jeremiah's written scroll, giving a concrete instance of the commentary's point that a page can be damaged or suppressed by human hands.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.28	scroll written again	After the king burns the scroll, Jeremiah is told to write its words again; the message outlasts a vulnerable sheet, paralleling the commentary's contrast between fragile writing and enduring speech.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.16	book of remembrance and the divine name	Malachi says a book of remembrance is written for those who fear the Lord and esteem his name; this links the commentary's fear, remembrance, prayerful naming, and preserved record.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.24.12	God-written tablets for instruction	The commentary distinguishes loose sheets from a single bound book; Exodus gives Moses tablets of stone with instruction written by God, a distinct durable written form associated with him.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.6.6	words on the heart	Moses commands that his words remain on Israel's heart, a direct scriptural counterpart to the commentary's word preserved in an instructed memory as well as on pages.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.6.9	words written on doorposts	The same instruction is to be written on house doorposts and gates; the verse supplies a concrete domestic written counterpart to words held in the heart.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hab.2.2	vision written to be read	Habakkuk is told to write the vision on tablets plainly so a reader can run with it; this joins the commentary's open writing surface to public reading and transmission.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Neh.8.8	reading and explanation of the book	The law is read from the book and interpreted so the hearers understand; this illuminates the commentary's messenger who voices written pages rather than relying on silent inspection alone.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.16	one person's guilt is not another's	The law forbids putting children to death for parents' crimes; it gives a legal form of the first rule quoted from Abraham's pages, that no bearer carries another's burden.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.18.20	the sinner bears his own guilt	Ezekiel says the child does not bear a parent's guilt and the person who sins bears that person's own consequence; this develops the commentary's individual-accountability reading of the old pages.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.31.30	each dies for their own sin	Jeremiah answers the inherited sour-grapes proverb by saying each person dies for their own sin, a direct correction of the idea that one generation bears another's guilt.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.7.10	books opened for judgment	Daniel's heavenly court opens books before the judge; this is a close Jewish-scriptural counterpart to the commentary's pages opened at the end and deeds brought into judgment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	opened books and judgment by deeds	Revelation depicts books opened and the dead judged from what is written in them according to their deeds; it brings the commentary's opened pages and individual recompense together.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.3.3	writing on hearts rather than stone	Paul calls the Corinthians a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts, explicitly contrasting stone tablets and inward inscription; this gives a Christian reading of the commentary's two ways of keeping one word.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Heb.8.10	law written in minds and hearts	Hebrews applies Jeremiah's new-covenant promise of law written inwardly; it interprets Moses' external written instruction through the inward preservation that the commentary sets beside pages.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.5	holy ground at Moses' call	The Qur'anic Moses is summoned in a sacred valley before being sent to Pharaoh; Exodus also marks Moses' call by holy ground, while its burning-bush scene gives the encounter a different sign.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.3.10	Moses sent to Pharaoh	The commentary reads Moses' warning to Pharaoh as a model for the surah's admonition; Exodus likewise makes the encounter with Pharaoh the commission's stated purpose.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.5.2	Pharaoh asks who the Lord is	Exodus has Pharaoh ask who YHWH is and deny that he will heed him, whereas the commentary's Qur'anic Pharaoh claims the highest lordship for himself; the shared confrontation highlights different forms of defiance.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.7.11	Egyptian magicians reproduce a sign	Exodus' magicians reproduce Aaron's sign at first, while the commentary's Qur'anic magicians end by confessing faith after Moses' sign prevails; the same contest receives a sharply different human outcome.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.8.19	magicians recognize God's action	When unable to reproduce the plague, Pharaoh's magicians say it is God's finger, but the scene does not show them converting; the Qur'anic magicians' explicit submission makes that difference significant.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Exod.9.12	God hardens Pharaoh's heart	Exodus says God hardens Pharaoh's heart during the signs, adding divine hardening to the refusal that the commentary frames as Pharaoh's boast, denial, and turning away.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.12.1	Abraham leaves his land and father's house	The commentary praises the first-pages figure who left the inherited path; Genesis begins Abraham's call by commanding him to leave country, kin, and father's house, though it does not itself mention idol-breaking.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Ezek.20.18	refusal to follow ancestral idols	The commentary contrasts an old warning with mere appeal to ancestors; Ezekiel tells the next generation not to follow their fathers' statutes or defile themselves with idols, making the break with inherited practice explicit.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.26.5	Abraham keeps commands before Moses	Genesis says Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept commandments, statutes, and teachings; it presents Abraham as already faithful to instruction before Moses, supporting the commentary's pairing of their earlier pages.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.18.19	Abraham teaches descendants justice	God says Abraham will command his children and household to keep the Lord's way by doing righteousness and justice; this makes his continuing legacy an ethical warning handed to later generations.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.15.5	stars as a promise of descendants	Genesis uses the night sky's stars to promise Abraham innumerable descendants, whereas the commentary's Abraham rejects celestial bodies that set; the shared star scene distinguishes a sign of promise from an object of worship.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 38:13	Abraham smashes his father's idols	The midrash expands Abraham's rejection of ancestral worship into the story of breaking the idols in Terah's shop; it makes explicit the departure from inherited custom that the commentary stresses.
strong	tevrat	paralel	Jubilees 12:1–8	Abram rejects the household idols	Jubilees has Abram challenge his father over the idols and their worship; this Second Temple retelling supplies the explicit anti-idolatry background behind the commentary's contrast between Abraham and his ancestors.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 44:12	Abraham taken beyond astrology	The midrash reads God's taking Abraham outside to see the stars as release from astrological destiny; it adds a Jewish interpretation to the commentary's scene where Abraham watches heavenly bodies set and seeks God's guidance.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Berakhot 26b	Abraham institutes morning prayer	The Talmud derives the morning prayer from Abraham rising early to stand before God; this interpretive tradition connects the commentary's Abrahamic prayer with its account of the purified person remembering God's name and praying.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 44:20	Abraham keeps the law and covenant	Sirach remembers Abraham as keeping the law of the Most High and entering covenant; this Jewish praise makes the Abraham-Moses pairing a continuity of divine instruction, not merely shared antiquity.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 45:1	Moses' blessed memory among later generations	Sirach says Moses is beloved and his memory is blessed; it gives a Jewish witness to the commentary's closing image of Moses' name preserved among those who come later.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 6:2	engraved tablets read as freedom	The Mishnah plays on the engraved writing of the tablets as freedom for those who study Torah; it turns Moses' written pages into a formative, liberating instruction rather than inert text.
medium	tevrat	paralel	Josephus, Antiquities 1.7.1	Abraham argues for one creator	Josephus portrays Abraham challenging inherited polytheism and teaching that one God created the universe; this Jewish retelling gives the commentary's rejection of ancestral custom an explicit monotheistic argument.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Acts.7.2	Abraham called from Mesopotamia	Stephen retells Abraham's call as occurring in Mesopotamia before he settled in Haran; the Christian retelling emphasizes that the patriarch's path begins by leaving his natal setting.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Heb.11.8	Abraham departs by faith	Hebrews says Abraham obeyed the call and went out without knowing his destination; its interpretation makes the departure from inherited security an act of trust in God's guidance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.3.9	ancestry does not guarantee Abraham's way	John the Baptist rejects reliance on having Abraham as father and says God can raise children from stones; this directly supports the commentary's claim that old ancestry alone is no measure of truth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.8.39	Abraham's children must do Abraham's works	Jesus answers a claim of descent by requiring Abraham's works; it sharpens the commentary's contrast between honoring the ancient patriarch and simply repeating ancestral custom.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.29	Moses and the prophets are to be heard	In the parable Abraham says the brothers have Moses and the prophets and should listen to them; the old written testimony is presented as sufficient warning to people who turn away.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.31	a risen messenger cannot force belief	Abraham says those who refuse Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by someone rising from the dead; this intensifies the commentary's claim that the old pages already confront the rejecter.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.5.46	Moses wrote about Jesus	Jesus says Moses wrote about him; this Christian reading makes Moses' written testimony a witness to a later messenger, like the commentary's old pages bearing a warning read anew.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.5.47	failure to believe Moses' writings	Jesus asks how hearers will believe his words if they do not believe Moses' writings; the verse directly stages the commentary's contrast between written warning and refusal to hear it.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.4.17	Jesus reads an opened scroll	Jesus receives and opens Isaiah's scroll in the synagogue; the scene gives a concrete Christian instance of a messenger voicing an old written page to a present audience.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Luke.4.21	old writing announced as fulfilled now	After reading Isaiah, Jesus says the scripture is fulfilled in the hearers' hearing; this Christian interpretation shows how an old page can be presented as a current warning or promise.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.25	Moses chooses affliction over passing pleasure	Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people rather than temporary enjoyment in Pharaoh's house; it concretely parallels the commentary's preference for the lasting afterlife over worldly life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.26	Moses values future reward above Egypt's riches	Hebrews says Moses counted reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward; this interprets the same choice of lasting good over present advantage that the commentary sees in Moses' magicians.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.20	treasure stored in heaven	Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where decay and theft cannot destroy it; this gives a direct ethical counterpart to preferring the more enduring hereafter over worldly life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.2.17	world passes, God's will remains	John contrasts the passing world and its desire with the one who does God's will abiding forever; this closely matches the commentary's contrast between the transient present and what lasts.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.6	judgment according to each person's deeds	Paul says God repays each according to works; this Christian formulation joins the commentary's reading of the pages' rule that each person's striving is seen and fully requited.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.8	each receives wages for own labor	Paul says each worker receives wages according to that worker's labor; this is a close match for the pages' claim that a person has only what they strive for and receives recompense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.5	each bears their own load	Paul says each will carry their own load, a concise Christian counterpart to the commentary's first rule that no bearer takes another's burden.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.18	visible things are temporary, unseen things eternal	Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; it gives a Christian formulation of the commentary's choice between the fading present and lasting hereafter.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.3.3	Spirit's letter written on human hearts	Paul calls the community a letter written by the Spirit on hearts rather than with ink on stone tablets; this directly interprets the commentary's two modes of preserving one utterance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.8.10	law written in minds and hearts	Hebrews applies Jeremiah's new-covenant promise of law written inwardly; it interprets Moses' external written instruction through the inward preservation that the commentary sets beside pages.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.24	flesh is like grass that withers	Peter quotes the grass and flower that fade, matching the commentary's pasture that dries and is swept away while the word remains.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.1.25	the Lord's word remains forever	Peter applies Isaiah's enduring word to the proclaimed gospel; this adds a Christian reading of the old word as surviving through present recitation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.9.48	Isaiah's unquenched fire as warning	Mark applies Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire to Gehenna; Isaiah speaks of corpses and worms, while Mark makes the image an eschatological warning, a useful contrast to the Qur'anic person who neither dies nor lives.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Isa.66.24	undying worm and unquenched fire	Isaiah describes corpses of rebels exposed to worms and fire, not a person who neither dies nor lives; the shared fire image clarifies the distinct afterlife claim made in the commentary.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.34.4	heavens rolled like a scroll	Isaiah pictures the host of heaven falling as the sky rolls up like a scroll; this is the opposite cosmic motion to the pages spread open in the commentary's cited end-time scene.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.6.14	sky withdrawn like a rolled scroll	Revelation says the sky vanished like a scroll being rolled up; alongside the commentary's opened pages, it supplies the paired image of cosmic writing rolled shut.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.3	tree planted by water remains fruitful	The psalm's watered tree whose leaf does not wither contrasts with the commentary's pasture that dries; its righteous-tree image also gives a counterpart to the surah's successful purified person.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.4	wicked as windblown chaff	The psalm likens the wicked to chaff driven away, a specific plant-and-wind image that complements the commentary's pasture withering and the rejecter facing loss.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.15	human life like grass and a flower	The psalm says human life flourishes briefly like field grass and then disappears; it makes the commentary's contrast between the temporary worldly life and enduring revelation concrete.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.103.17	steadfast love endures across generations	Against the fading human life, the psalm says the Lord's steadfast love is everlasting for those who fear him; this joins the commentary's fear, permanence, and transmission to later generations.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.78.6	teaching passed to children not yet born	The psalm says the next generation should know the teaching and tell it to their children; this gives a scriptural model for old warning surviving through later hearers.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.56.8	tears kept in God's book	The psalm asks God to keep the speaker's tears in a bottle and record them in a book; it gives the commentary's divine book of old generations a personal image of what God does not forget.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.139.16	days recorded in God's book	The psalm says the speaker's days were written in God's book before they came to be; this parallels Moses' statement that the earliest generations are held in a book with God.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.1	names written in the book at the end	Daniel says deliverance comes for those found written in the book; it links a preserved written record to the final fate that the commentary says the first pages describe.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.34.10	Moses remembered as an unsurpassed prophet	Deuteronomy closes by saying no prophet like Moses arose, whom the Lord knew face to face; it gives a biblical form of the lasting recognition of Moses' name at the end of the surah.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.8.16	testimony bound and instruction sealed	Isaiah commands the testimony to be bound up and instruction sealed among disciples; this gives another image of a warning preserved in writing for a faithful community.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.36.28	rewriting a burned warning	Jeremiah is told to write again the words of the burned scroll; the repeated row emphasizes the commentary's contrast between the vulnerable page and a message that survives its destruction.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:WLC:Exod.17.14	written memorial and oral remembrance	Moses is told to write God's judgment against Amalek in a book and recite it to Joshua; this joins a written record to spoken transmission as the commentary does.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:WLC:Gen.15.6	Abraham's belief counted as righteousness	Genesis says Abraham trusted God and was counted righteous; it supplies a specific biblical account of Abraham's response to divine promise behind the commentary's image of him as a model for the successful purified person.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:WLC:Exod.8.19	Egyptian magicians concede divine action	The magicians call the plague God's finger when they cannot reproduce it; set beside the Qur'anic magicians' confession, this repeated row emphasizes that Exodus gives recognition without the same narrated surrender.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:WLC:Ps.1.4	chaff driven away	The psalm's wicked are chaff the wind drives off, a close image for the commentary's withered pasture swept away and its rejecter separated from the successful person.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:WLC:Ps.1.3	leaf that does not wither	The psalm's righteous tree has an unwithered leaf, providing a specific counter-image to the commentary's fading pasture and a durable life associated with right conduct.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.1.1	God spoke to ancestors through prophets	Hebrews describes the one God speaking to the ancestors through prophets in many portions and ways; this supports reading the named earlier pages as distinct witnesses within a continuous message.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:WLC:Exod.3.10	Moses sent to Pharaoh	The second citation emphasizes that Moses is commissioned to confront Pharaoh, the scene the commentary uses to interpret admonition and refusal.
medium	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Luke.4.21	scripture fulfilled in the present hearing	Jesus interprets the Isaiah scroll he has just read as fulfilled in the audience's hearing; this adds a Christian example of an old written word made present through recitation.

text(r.output);

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.31.33	law written on hearts	Alongside the commentary's word kept in an instructed memory and in written pages, Jeremiah promises that God will write the law on the people's hearts, giving an explicit inward-inscription image.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.2.10	scroll written on both sides	Ezekiel sees a scroll covered on front and back with lamentation and woe; it adds a concrete written surface and prophetic warning to the commentary's individual pages.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.3.1	prophet eats the scroll before speaking	Ezekiel must eat the written scroll and then speak to Israel, joining page, mouth, and delivered warning in a way that complements the commentary's recited pages and remembered word.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.24	Moses completes the written law	Deuteronomy says Moses finished writing the words of the law in a book; this supplies the act of making the written witness that the commentary distinguishes from separate pages.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.2	Moses' teaching falls like rain on grass	In Moses' song, teaching is rain and speech dew that falls on grass and plants; this is a particular meeting of the commentary's Musa, recited word, and pasture imagery.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.39	Moses' song says God kills and makes alive	The same song declares that God kills and gives life, a direct Mosaic-scripture counterpart to the life-and-death claim the commentary finds among the old pages.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.55.11	word goes out and accomplishes its purpose	Isaiah says God's word does not return empty but achieves its work; beside the commentary's withering pasture and enduring pages, the verse makes the written warning effective, not merely preserved.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.12.8	Abraham calls on the Lord's name and worships	After arriving in Canaan, Abraham builds an altar and calls on the Lord's name; this is a concrete patriarchal instance of the commentary's remembered name joined to prayer.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Ezek.29.3	Pharaoh claims the Nile as his creation	Ezekiel depicts Pharaoh boasting that the Nile is his and that he made it, while the commentary sets Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord against the true creator; this gives the same arrogance a specifically Egyptian form.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.14	God brings every deed, even hidden ones, to judgment	Ecclesiastes says every work and hidden thing will be brought to judgment; this sharpens the commentary's reading of the pages as a record of each person's striving and recompense.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.24.12	God weighs the heart and repays each person	Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each according to deeds; this closely matches the commentary's reading that labor is seen and no one answers for another.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.32.32	Moses speaks of God's book	Moses asks to be blotted from God's book if Israel is not forgiven; this gives the commentary's book held with God a Mosaic setting, though Exodus uses it as a book of life rather than a record of the first generations.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.10.11	old events written as warning for the end	Paul says Israel's past events happened as examples and were written for admonition in the age's end; this directly matches the commentary's claim that the first pages remain a warning to present rejecters.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.15.4	earlier writings instruct and give hope	Paul says what was written beforehand was written for instruction and endurance; this Christian reading makes the commentary's old pages a present source of admonition and hope.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.25	earthly comfort reversed after death	Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus suffered, but now their conditions are reversed; this is a close parable counterpart to preferring the lasting afterlife over worldly life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.26	fixed chasm after judgment	Abraham says a great chasm prevents crossing between the two conditions; this adds the finality of the commentary's divided destinies after the present choice.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.46	two final outcomes, punishment and life	Jesus ends the judgment scene with eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other; this closely matches the commentary's contrast between the rejecter and the successful person.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.5.39	Scriptures testify about the messenger	Jesus says the Scriptures bear witness to him; this expands the nearby claim that Moses wrote about him and parallels the commentary's pages testifying to a warning delivered anew.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Luke.24.27	Moses and prophets interpreted as pointing forward	The risen Jesus interprets Moses and all the prophets from the Scriptures concerning himself; this is a Christian reading of earlier writings as a unified witness to a later message.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Luke.24.44	Moses, prophets, and psalms fulfilled together	Jesus names the Law of Moses, Prophets, and Psalms as writings that must be fulfilled; this supplies a distinct Christian account of separate earlier texts converging in one message.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Heb.11.24	Moses refuses Pharaoh's household identity	Hebrews says Moses refused to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son; this adds a specific act of rejecting the status of Pharaoh's house to the commentary's contrast between false lordship and allegiance to God.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.27	Moses leaves without fearing the king	Hebrews says Moses left Egypt by faith without fearing the king's anger; this complements the commentary's link between fear, guidance, and the choice to obey God's warning.
